expectedAnswer: Search the car without a warrant under the automobile exception, since there is probable cause to believe it contains contraband.
explanation: Seeing suspected drugs in plain view gave Officer Kelly probable cause that the vehicle contains contraband. Under the automobile exception (Carroll doctrine), the officer can search the vehicle (including containers within it that might hold the contraband) immediately without a warrant, due to the mobility of the vehicle and existing probable cause.

title: Scenario 87
scenario: During a lawful traffic stop at night, Officer Allen sees the driver nervously reaching under the seat. Fearing the driver might be accessing a weapon, Allen orders him out and conducts a quick search of the passenger compartment for weapons. A loaded pistol is found under the seat. Was this search legal?
questions: Yes. With specific suspicion the driver might be armed and dangerous, the officer can do a cursory protective search of the vehicle for weapons.
No. The officer needed a search warrant to look under the seat of the car.
No. The officer had no right to remove the driver from the vehicle during a traffic stop.
Yes. Cars have no expectation of privacy, so officers can always search them.
expectedAnswer: Yes. With specific suspicion the driver might be armed and dangerous, the officer can do a cursory protective search of the vehicle for weapons.
explanation: If an officer has reasonable suspicion that a detained driver or occupant is dangerous and may access a weapon, the officer can conduct a limited search of areas in the vehicle where a weapon might be hidden (a protective vehicle sweep). Here, the driver’s furtive movement justified checking under the seat for weapons, making the discovery of the pistol lawful.

title: Scenario 88
scenario: True or False: A suspect’s car is impounded for parking violations. During the standard inventory of the vehicle, an officer discovers narcotics hidden in a backpack in the trunk. This evidence is admissible in court.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: As long as the inventory search is conducted according to departmental policy (to catalog the vehicle’s contents for safekeeping, not as a pretext to find evidence), any contraband or evidence found during that procedure can be used in court. In this scenario, the officer’s discovery of narcotics in the trunk during a lawful inventory would be admissible.

title: Scenario 89
scenario: True or False: Routine booking questions (e.g., asking a suspect’s name, address, date of birth) do not require a Miranda warning because they are not aimed at eliciting incriminating evidence.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: Routine biographical questions asked during the booking process are exempt from Miranda. They are for administrative and identification purposes, not for gathering evidence of a crime. Therefore, officers can ask these basic questions without advising the suspect of the Miranda rights at that time.

title: Scenario 90
scenario: A homeowner invites officers inside to discuss a burglary. While inside, an officer asks, "Do you mind if we take a look around your house for any evidence?" The homeowner says, "Go ahead." The officers search and find stolen property. Later, the homeowner claims the search was illegal. What is the likely outcome?
questions: The search was legal because the homeowner voluntarily consented to it.
The search was illegal because the officers lacked a warrant.
The search was legal only if the officers had probable cause before asking for consent.
The search was illegal because the homeowner wasn’t informed of the right to refuse consent.
expectedAnswer: The search was legal because the homeowner voluntarily consented to it.
explanation: A search conducted pursuant to a person’s voluntary consent is lawful. The homeowner gave permission for the search, so no warrant or additional cause was required. Officers are not required to advise a person that they have the right to refuse consent (though consent must be freely given, not coerced).

title: Scenario 91
scenario: Officer Hall asks a homeowner for permission to search his house for evidence of a crime. The homeowner hesitates, so Hall says, "If you don’t let us in, I’ll come back with a warrant and make things difficult for you." The homeowner then says, "Fine, go ahead." The search yields evidence. In court, the defense challenges the consent. What is likely to happen?
questions: The consent may be deemed involuntary, because it was obtained through a coercive threat of a warrant, and the evidence could be suppressed.
The consent is valid; the officer was just explaining the inevitable outcome.
The evidence is admissible because the homeowner ultimately said "go ahead".
The consent is irrelevant since officers could have gotten a warrant anyway.
expectedAnswer: The consent may be deemed involuntary, because it was obtained through a coercive threat of a warrant, and the evidence could be suppressed.
explanation: Consent must be freely and voluntarily given. Here, the officer’s statement was coercive – threatening to “make things difficult” – which can invalidate the consent. A court would likely find that the homeowner’s consent was not truly voluntary, and thus the evidence discovered would be suppressed.

title: Scenario 92
scenario: True or False: Only a person with a reasonable expectation of privacy in the area searched can challenge the legality of a search in court.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: This is the principle of “standing.” A defendant can only contest a search if it violated their own reasonable expectation of privacy. For example, one generally can’t object to the search of someone else’s property, because the intrusion did not invade their personal privacy rights.

title: Scenario 93
scenario: True or False: In California, private citizens who are not police officers are not bound by the Fourth Amendment, so evidence they discover and hand over to police (without being asked to search) is generally admissible.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: The Fourth Amendment restricts government actors, not private individuals acting on their own. If a private person finds evidence and turns it over to police without being at the direction of police, the evidence is admissible. (However, if the citizen was acting as an agent of law enforcement, Fourth Amendment rules would apply.)

title: Scenario 94
scenario: True or False: If officers conduct an unlawful search of a home but later discover the same evidence lawfully via an independent source, the evidence may still be admissible despite the initial illegality.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: The “independent source” doctrine is an exception to the exclusionary rule. It holds that evidence initially discovered during an unlawful search can still be admitted if it is later obtained independently by legal means untainted by the original illegality. Similarly, the “inevitable discovery” doctrine allows evidence if it would have been found inevitably by lawful means. These exceptions prevent suppressing evidence that the police obtained separately from any misconduct.

title: Scenario 95
scenario: True or False: Probation and parole searches are intended to ensure compliance with the terms of release and do not require the officer to have separate reasonable suspicion or a warrant.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: Persons on probation or parole with search conditions have significantly reduced privacy rights. Officers can generally search them (and areas under their control) without warrants or additional suspicion, as long as the search is not arbitrary or harassment. These conditions are part of the individual’s agreement for remaining in the community under supervision.

title: Scenario 96
scenario: True or False: The exclusionary rule is meant to deter police misconduct by excluding illegally obtained evidence, even if that means a guilty person might go free.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: The exclusionary rule’s primary purpose is to deter law enforcement from violating constitutional rights. It does so by removing the incentive to conduct illegal searches or seizures, since any evidence obtained unlawfully can be thrown out in court. This can sometimes result in a person escaping conviction due to lack of admissible evidence, but the rule is considered necessary to uphold constitutional protections.

title: Scenario 97
scenario: True or False: An officer can lawfully seize evidence that is in plain view as long as the officer is in a place they have a right to be and it’s immediately apparent the item is contraband or evidence of a crime.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: The plain view doctrine allows officers to seize evidence without a warrant if three conditions are met: the officer is lawfully present in the location, the item is in plain sight, and the officer immediately recognizes the item as contraband or evidence. Under those circumstances, picking up the item does not violate the Fourth Amendment because no additional search occurs.

title: Scenario 98
scenario: True or False: A peace officer in California cannot make an arrest for an infraction (like a traffic infraction) because infractions are not punishable by jail time.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: In general, infractions (such as most minor traffic violations) are not arrestable offenses – they are handled by citation (ticket) since the only punishment is a fine. There are limited exceptions (e.g., if a person refuses to sign a promise to appear or there’s no satisfactory identification, an officer might arrest to ensure appearance in court), but typically infractions do not result in physical arrest.

title: Scenario 99
scenario: True or False: If a person commits a misdemeanor in an officer’s presence, the officer can arrest them then and there without a warrant.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: Misdemeanors committed in the presence of a peace officer can be the basis for an immediate warrantless arrest (Penal Code §836). The officer directly observed the crime, which satisfies the requirement for warrantless misdemeanor arrests. (If the misdemeanor is not in the officer’s presence, an arrest warrant or a private person’s arrest is generally required, absent statutory exceptions.)

title: Scenario 100
scenario: True or False: A landlord’s valid consent to search a tenant’s apartment is not sufficient; generally, only the tenant (or someone with common authority over the apartment) can give lawful consent to search the tenant’s private space.
questions: True
False
expectedAnswer: True
explanation: A landlord cannot usually consent to a police search of a tenant’s dwelling because the tenant has a reasonable expectation of privacy there. Consent must come from someone who actually has common authority or control over the space (like a co-occupant). There are narrow exceptions (e.g., property owner consent for common areas), but a landlord’s consent to search a rented apartment is not valid against the tenant’s privacy interest.
